message.content:
I don’t have a way to directly measure your current internet connection from here. However, you can quickly find out your upload/download speeds yourself! Here’s how:

### 1. Use an Online Speed Test  
- **Speedtest.net** – Visit [speedtest.net](https://www.speedtest.net/) and click “Go.”  
- **Fast.com** – Go to [fast.com](https://fast.com/); it automatically starts testing your download speed.  
- **Google Speed Test** – Search “internet speed test” on Google and use the built‑in test.

These sites will show:
- **Download speed** (how fast data comes into your device).  
- **Upload speed** (how fast data goes out).  
- **Ping / latency** (delay between your device and the server).

### 2. Command‑Line Speed Test (if you prefer terminal)  
If you’re comfortable with the command line, you can install `speedtest-cli`:

#### On Windows (PowerShell)
```powershell
pip install speedtest-cli
speedtest
```

#### On macOS/Linux (Terminal)
```bash
sudo apt-get install speedtest-cli   # Debian/Ubuntu
brew install speedtest-cli           # macOS with Homebrew
speedtest
```

This will output your download/upload speeds and ping.

### 3. Check Your Router’s Admin Page  
Most routers display current throughput statistics on their admin interface. Log in to your router (usually at `192.168.0.1`, `192.168.1.1`, or similar) and look for a “Status” or “Internet” section.

---

**Tip:** Run the test a few times at different times of day to see how traffic patterns affect your speed. If you consistently get lower speeds than what your ISP promises, consider contacting them or troubleshooting potential issues (e.g., cable connections, firmware updates, interference).

Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the results or troubleshooting specific problems!
